title: How to Train Your Agent: Building Reliable Agents with RL — Kyle Corbitt, OpenPipe
talk_summary: OpenPipe's Kyle Corbitt describes fine-tuning a small Qwen 2.5 14B model with RL to answer email-inbox questions, beating prompted frontier models on accuracy, cost, and latency. The transferable lessons are about building realistic environments, verifiable reward functions, and watching for reward hacking—not about RL training itself.

takeaways.technique: Golden-answer dataset from inverted task generation
takeaways.what_they_do: They took real email batches, had Gemini 2.5 Pro generate realistic questions whose answers were in those emails, filtered for realism, and kept a few thousand question/answer/source triples as a verified eval set.
takeaways.numbers: a few thousand questions with verified answers

takeaways.what_they_do: They used a simple LLM judge to compare agent answer to golden answer, but iterated on the judge until it was well calibrated on what counts as correct.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we did have to do a little bit of uh iteration there making sure that the judge was well calibrated on like what you know what what counts as as correct

takeaways.what_they_do: They inspect actual agent rollouts rather than trusting the score, and found models exploiting verifier bugs (e.g., putting every word in every category) or collapsing to one output.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to be looking at your your rollouts, not just blindly trusting the reward function, figuring out what's actually happening

takeaways.technique: Penalize extra turns / tool calls in scoring
takeaways.what_they_do: They added a small extra-credit term for fewer back-and-forth tool turns, so among correct answers the agent preferred cheaper, lower-latency paths.
takeaways.evidence_quote: between two answers that both get it right, we would rather it took fewer turns back and forth because that's fewer tokens, that's lower latency, lower costs
takeaways.numbers: spiked to over six turns early, then beat prompted models on turn count

takeaways.technique: Penalize confident wrong answers over abstention
takeaways.what_they_do: They rewarded 'I don't know' more than a wrong confident answer, cutting hallucination rate well below prompted models.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's much better to say, hey, I don't know, than to make up an answer

takeaways.what_they_do: They insist on maximizing prompted-model performance and fixing environment/tool bugs before considering training, because training masks environment bugs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I would generally always recommend starting with getting the best performance you can with a prompted model before going to any training
